clue.text: See 2
It's all over in Nashville: deft hit "G.I. Blues" — All Shook Up!

indicators.note: the title of an Elvis hit doubles as an instruction to shake up the preceding letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: In Nashville, Elvis's songs G.I. Blues and All Shook Up mark the end of an era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All Shook Up' signals the anagram of NASHVILLEDEFTHITGIBLUES, all 23 letters. The phrase was announced after Elvis Presley's concerts to tell fans the show was over.
explanation.definitionFit: The announcement made at the close of Presley's concerts became an idiom meaning the show is finished and nothing more will happen.

clue.text: Japanese drink, about a quarter, making one legless

indicators.note: the rice wine goes around the compass letter, enclosing it

parts.note: sake is Japanese rice wine
N, north, is one of the four quarters or cardinal points of the compass

explanation.surface: Drinking Japanese rice wine for a quarter of an hour leaves someone unable to stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legless' is British slang for very drunk, which the surface plays on; here it literally means having no legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A serpent is a reptile with no limbs at all, so it is literally a creature without legs.

clue.text: Two events in one for cycle, sites of 2004 and 1948 Olympics half-completed

parts.note: bi is the prefix put before cycle to make bicycle

indicators.note: only half of each city's name is finished, so each loses its last three letters

parts.note: Athens hosted the 2004 Summer Olympics
London hosted the 1948 Summer Olympics

explanation.surface: A two-sport contest with cycling, staged partly in two former Olympic host cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-completed' keeps only the first half of each city's name, ATH from ATHENS and LON from LONDON.
explanation.definitionFit: A biathlon is a single competition combining two disciplines, typically cross-country skiing and rifle shooting.

clue.text: Worry about the Queen's nose

indicators.note: the word for worry wraps around the royal abbreviation

parts.note: to fret is to worry
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone frets over the shape of the monarch's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nose' looks like a noun but is the verb, to nose about.
explanation.definitionFit: To ferret is to search about inquisitively, as does someone who noses into things.

clue.text: Brave soldier shunned amid shout of encouragement for knight

indicators.note: the shortened brave word sits in the middle of the shout

parts.note: a cheer is a shout of encouragement

indicators.note: the soldier is avoided, so it is taken out of the word for brave

parts.note: valiant means brave
a soldier ant is a kind of ant, so ant can stand for soldier

explanation.surface: A courageous soldier ignored amid the cheering crowd as a knight is hailed.
explanation.walkthrough: A soldier ant is a caste of ant, which lets 'soldier' stand for ANT; the surface's brave soldier is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Chevalier is the French title for a knight, also used in English for a member of certain orders of knighthood.

clue.text: Rising duck problem becomes material

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the letters are read upwards, so the whole run is reversed

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, nil
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: A question about why a duck climbs turns into a matter of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' turns NILSUM upwards to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Muslin is a fine, loosely woven cotton fabric, a kind of cloth or material.

clue.text: Country landowner making life arrangement, but married, not I!

indicators.note: making signals that the following letters are formed into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letter I is taken out of the pool, as 'not I' says

explanation.surface: A rural landlord fixes up a life plan, but he is the one married, not me.
explanation.walkthrough: Add M (married) to LIFEARRANGEMENT and remove I ('not I'); the remaining letters rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentleman farmer is someone who owns and runs a country estate, typically for pleasure rather than income.

clue.text: Plant at awkward angle with part of fork

indicators.note: an awkward angle is one bent out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a tine is a prong of a fork

explanation.surface: A plant sticks out at a strange angle beside a garden fork's prong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges ANGLE to EGLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweet briar, a wild rose, which is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Place for bingo

definitions.meaning: a dwelling or home, as in 'come round to my place'
the game is also known as housey-housey, and the call made on winning names it too

explanation.definitionFit: A home is a place to live, and the number game of bingo has long been called by the same name.

clue.text: Bush dense here, stupid (and abroad)

parts.note: thick is informal for stupid
et is French for and, so it is and in a foreign language

explanation.surface: An aside on a foolish politician named Bush, said by someone overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking of President Bush being called stupid; 'Bush' is really shrubbery.
explanation.definitionFit: A thicket is a dense growth of shrubs, a place where bushes grow close together.

clue.text: Little flower with dull centre held by pin

indicators.note: the middle letters are grasped inside the fastener

parts.note: a rivet is a metal pin used to fasten plates together

indicators.note: the centre of a four-letter word is its two middle letters

explanation.surface: A small bloom with a dreary middle, fixed in place by a pin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is something that flows, not a bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: A rivulet is a small stream, a little thing that flows.

clue.text: Laugh at Archimedes' fourth eureka

indicators.note: the fourth letter of the mathematician's name is taken

parts.note: aha is an exclamation of discovery, like eureka

explanation.surface: Mocking Archimedes for his fourth cry of eureka.
explanation.walkthrough: Archimedes is said to have shouted eureka on discovering displacement in his bath, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeated ha is the conventional written form of laughter.

clue.text: Undesirable result of constitutional breakdown in the end?

definitions.text: Undesirable result of constitutional breakdown in the end?

parts.words: Undesirable result of constitutional breakdown in the end?
parts.note: read as politics this is the collapse of a state's constitution; really it is digestion breaking down food, with a gaseous result emerging from the rear end

explanation.definitionFit: Wind in the gut is an unwanted by-product of digestion, released from the bottom.

clue.text: At Portsmouth, then another team

indicators.note: another signals a different version of the preceding letters, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Away at Portsmouth one week, then facing another football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' rearranges ATPORTSMOUTHTHEN; Portsmouth is itself a football club, which makes 'another team' fit the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Tottenham Hotspur is a professional football club based in north London.

clue.text: About to become bachelors, blow it!

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts, so BAs are bachelors
about to happen means happening soon

explanation.surface: Someone about to graduate exclaims in frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blow it!' looks like a curse, but describes an instrument you blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A bassoon is a woodwind instrument, played by blowing into its reed.

clue.text: Pacific character of a drug, amphetamine, being reversed

indicators.note: the run of a, the drug and the amphetamine is read backwards

parts.note: E is short for ecstasy, the drug
speed is slang for amphetamine

explanation.surface: The calm nature of someone on drugs is undone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being reversed' turns AESPEED around. 'Pacific' looks like peaceful but is the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific is an ocean, so it has a deep-sea nature, out far from shore.

clue.text: All of the pack and then some seaman

parts.note: a deck is the whole pack of playing cards
a hand is some of the cards, those dealt to one player

explanation.surface: A sailor takes the whole pack of cards and more besides.
explanation.definitionFit: A deckhand is a sailor who works on the deck of a ship.

clue.text: Ticks off after this run-through?

parts.note: sounds like checking items after a rehearsal; really the parasitic ticks fall off a flock after it has been driven through a disinfectant bath

explanation.definitionFit: Farmers drive their flocks through an insecticidal bath to kill parasites such as ticks.

clue.text: This compiler's game, which is not virtuous?

parts.note: the setter refers to himself, I am, shortened to I'm
patience is a card game for one player

explanation.surface: The setter plays a card game and wonders whether that is a virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: Patience is proverbially a virtue, so its opposite is not virtuous.
explanation.definitionFit: Since patience is a virtue, being restless and unwilling to wait is its unvirtuous opposite.

clue.text: Author eating nutty, smelly stuff

indicators.note: the author's name takes the crazy word inside it

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American author
nutty means mad

explanation.surface: A writer munches something nutty and pungent.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomade is a scented ointment for the hair, so it is fragrant stuff.

clue.text: Sounds like a company car

definitions.meaning: a companion, someone who keeps you company, especially at a social event
the Ford model of that name, long a typical British company car

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like a' just links the two senses; the Ford of that name was a stock company car.
explanation.definitionFit: A companion who accompanies someone is one sense, and a long-running Ford car model is the other.

clue.text: Two thirds weak reversed to get brawn

indicators.note: the shortened weak word is read backwards
only two thirds of the six-letter word is kept, so its last two letters go

parts.note: feeble means weak

explanation.surface: Turning weakness around to gain strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two thirds' cuts FEEBLE to FEEB; 'reversed' turns it.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is informal for muscular strength, the same as brawn.

clue.text: Paddy finds last of beer in bar

indicators.note: the final letter goes inside the word for bar

parts.note: to stop is to bar or block

indicators.note: the final letter of the drink's name is taken

explanation.surface: An Irishman finishes his beer in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like a nickname for an Irishman, but is British slang for a fit of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A strop and a paddy are both British informal words for a sulky temper tantrum.

clue.text: March sunny? Not entirely — diabolical

parts.note: a demo is a demonstration, a protest march

indicators.note: the pleasant word is incomplete, so its last letter goes

parts.note: nice describes sunny weather

explanation.surface: Is March sunny? Not quite: the weather is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month but is a protest; 'Not entirely' trims NICE to NIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Demonic means of or like a demon, which is the same as devilish or diabolical.

clue.text: See 15
Lady Diana manipulated?

indicators.note: the name is handled and reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Was Princess Diana manipulated by others?
explanation.definitionFit: Nadia is a woman's first name, so it fits a lady.

clue.text: To arrange willy-nilly, which Mandelson and Ayling did, is accepted

indicators.note: the short word is taken in by the phrase built from the two men's job

parts.note: Peter Mandelson and Bob Ayling ran the Millennium Dome in London, so they ran Dome

explanation.surface: Two figures of the Millennium Dome project ran things at random, it is claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Millennium Dome was a troubled exhibition building in London for the year 2000; IS goes inside RAN DOME.
explanation.definitionFit: To randomise is to put things in an order determined by chance, arranging them haphazardly.
